content: Patients with advanced laryngeal cancer who exhibit poor functional status, such as severe airway compromise necessitating tracheostomy or enteric feeding, are generally unsuitable candidates for laryngeal preservation. A review of the literature identified 16 studies encompassing 1,180 cases, with a focus on thyroid gland invasion as a significant risk factor. Among 399 total laryngectomy specimens analyzed, 33 cases (8%) demonstrated thyroid gland invasion. The subsites of these cases included glottic (7 cases), transglottic (8 cases), subglottic (5 cases), and supraglottic (3 cases) locations, with 10 cases lacking specific subsite information. In 94% of cases, thyroid gland invasion occurred via direct extension, while lymphatic spread was observed in only one specimen. The method of invasion was not recorded in 15 specimens. In 23 cases, subglottic extension was noted, and in all instances, the extension exceeded 10 mm. Significant risk factors for thyroid gland invasion included subglottic extension, transglottic tumors, and cartilage invasion. Two studies also analyzed cartilage invasion, which was found to be a significant risk factor. For glottic cancer with clinically positive neck nodes (N+), therapeutic neck dissection should include at least ipsilateral neck levels II, III, and IV. Elective contralateral neck dissection is not routinely recommended for ipsilateral N+ glottic cancer. Radical or modified radical neck dissection may be considered based on the extent of nodal metastasis. Ipsilateral levels II, III, and IV are most commonly involved in cervical metastasis of advanced glottic cancers, while levels I and V are rarely affected. Dissection of levels I or V may be considered based on individual nodal status. The clinical efficacy and safety of super-selective neck dissection in clinically N+ glottic cancer have not yet been fully evaluated. For clinically negative necks (N0) in glottic cancer, elective neck dissection is not routinely recommended for T1N0 and T2N0 cases but should be considered for T3N0 and T4N0 cases. Elective neck dissection for T3N0 and T4N0 glottic cancer should include ipsilateral neck levels II, III, and IV. Elective treatment of the neck is justified if the risk of occult lymph node metastasis exceeds 15%. For early glottic cancer, elective neck dissection is not recommended due to the low risk of nodal involvement. However, it is acceptable for advanced glottic cancers without clinical neck metastasis (T3N0 and T4N0). Some studies suggest that meticulous follow-up observation for T3N0 glottic cancer can yield survival rates comparable to those of initial neck treatment. For supraglottic cancer, conservative laryngeal surgery, such as open partial laryngectomy or transoral laser/robotic surgery, is recommended for T1/T2 cases. If surgical exposure is inadequate during transoral surgery, conversion to another treatment option, such as radiation therapy or open partial laryngectomy, should be considered. Open partial laryngectomy provides excellent local control but may result in significant aspiration and postoperative dysphagia, often requiring tracheostomy and feeding tubes during the early postoperative period. Transoral laryngeal surgery offers comparable oncologic outcomes with superior functional results, including reduced postoperative morbidity and shorter hospital stays. For T3/T4 supraglottic cancers, total laryngectomy is the primary surgical treatment. Partial laryngectomy may be performed in selected cases without extensive tongue base invasion, bilateral cricoarytenoid unit impairment, or inferior extension to the cricoid cartilage, though it carries a higher risk of postoperative morbidity. Conservative laryngeal surgery may be used for functional larynx preservation in T3/T4 tumors without extensive involvement, while total laryngectomy remains the preferred treatment for tumors with extensive invasion. Management of neck lymph nodes in supraglottic cancer differs from glottic cancer due to the earlier involvement of the lymphatic system and higher prevalence of nodal metastases. Therapeutic neck dissection should include at least levels II, III, and IV for clinically positive necks (N+). Selective neck dissection may be appropriate for patients with limited nodal pathology. For clinically negative necks (N0), elective ipsilateral neck dissection should be considered, particularly for advanced-stage tumors or those with midline crossing. Selective neck dissection of levels II, III, and IV is preferred over comprehensive dissection for clinically N0 cases. The decision to perform elective neck dissection should consider the risk of occult metastases, which varies widely depending on clinical, imaging, and histopathological methods. Postoperative management of laryngeal cancer patients requires careful assessment and management of factors predisposing to complications. Wound infection may present with erythema, edema, fever, foul odor, and elevated leukocyte count. Pharyngocutaneous fistula should be suspected in patients with fever and tense, erythematous skin flaps in the suprastomal region after total laryngectomy. Comorbidities such as diabetes, hepatic disease, anemia, and malnutrition, as well as the use of immunosuppressive medications, increase the risk of complications.
